title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature

match.reason: The closest bank point, Literature from different contexts, teaches context in general and mentions First Nations authors only in passing, while the new point is about the distinctive features of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature, and the other bank point is written for Year 8 and focuses on values.

draft.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature includes stories, poems, plays and memoirs written by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors. A memoir is a true account of part of the author's own life.
Country
For many First Nations peoples, Country means the land, waters and sky that a person belongs to and cares for. It is more than a place on a map. Many authors write about their connection to Country.
Family and language
Many works also draw on family, community and the author's language. A writer may include words from their own language or write about Elders and relatives.
Storytelling
First Nations peoples have told stories for a very long time, in speech, song, dance and art. Many writers draw on these traditions, so their work can carry knowledge handed down over generations.
draft.remember: Many First Nations authors write about Country, family, language and long traditions of storytelling.

a.q: A memoir by a Torres Strait Islander author describes growing up on her island, her grandmother's teaching and her home language. What does this show about the writing?
opts: It draws on Country, family and language
It is a made-up story with no link to real life
It avoids mentioning any place or relatives
It is written only to explain a school subject
a.why: The memoir centres on her island home, her grandmother and her language, which are common themes in First Nations writing. It is not made up, because a memoir is a true account of the author's own life.
a.clue: Look at the place, the grandmother and the language.

b.q: Jarrah, a Year 7 student, reads a poem by a First Nations author that uses a few words from the author's own language. Why might the author have done this?
opts: To show the importance of language to identity
To make the poem harder for anyone to read
To follow a rule that all poems need them
To replace the need for any English words
b.why: Language is one of the things many First Nations authors draw on, so using it shows its importance to who they are. It is not a rule for every poem, and the words are not there to shut readers out.
b.clue: Think about what language means to a community.

a.best: It draws on Country, family and language

b.best: To show the importance of language to identity

problems.detail: The card says writers may include words from their own language, but it never links language to identity or says why a writer does this. The answer relies on an idea the card does not teach, though a student can partly infer it.

check.summary: The card, the remember line and question a are accurate and clear. Question b's answer depends on linking language to identity, which the card does not teach; consider adding a sentence on why writers use their own language.
